title: Asking questions: seven question words
title_target: Apa, sapa, ngendi, kapan, pira, piyé, ngapa
goal: Master the whole Javanese question toolkit in one unit — seven question words, how to make yes-no questions, and how to ask someone to repeat when you didn't catch the answer.
bekal: using the seven question words and their krama partners
making yes-no questions with *apa* or with intonation alone
asking for a repeat without sounding stiff: *pripun?*, *nyuwun sewu, malih?*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kelangan HP
dialogs.intro: Dian has lost her *HP* (a mobile phone, in Indonesian usage). Rini fires question after question at her — the perfect situation to see all seven question words at work. A fast ngoko conversation, no small talk.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ora ngerti. Mau ésuk isih ana.
lines.id: I don't know. It was still there this morning.
lines.literal: not know. earlier morning still exist.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: Where all did you go today?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: To campus, then to the warung.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Sing pungkasan kowé nyekel HP kapan?
lines.id: When did you last have your phone?
lines.literal: which last you hold phone when?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: At the warung, when I was paying.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Wah, mesthi kèri ing kono. Sapa sing jaga?
lines.id: Then you must have left it there. Who's working there?
lines.literal: wow, surely left-behind at there. who which guard?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Bu Sri. How do I ask her?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: Easy. Come on, I'll take you there now.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Matur nuwun, Rin. Kowé pancèn kanca sing apik.
lines.id: Thanks, Rin. You really are a good friend.
lines.literal: thanks, Rin. you indeed friend which good.

notes: **Kena apa** means "why" — literally "hit by what", what happened to it. Other forms with the same meaning: *ngapa*, *geneya*, *kenèng apa*. The krama is *kénging punapa*. Of all of them, *ngapa* is the shortest and the most common.
**Rai** means "face". The respectful word is *pasuryan* (krama inggil), and *rai* is also used in plain krama. Using the ngoko word *rai* for a respected person's face sounds rude; use *pasuryan*.
**Banjur** means "then, after that"; the krama is *lajeng*. It is the most common word for linking events in sequence, and it comes back in unit 20.
**Nalika** means "when, at the time"; the krama is also *nalika*. More casual forms: *pas* (borrowed from Indonesian) and *wektu*.
**Kèri** means "left behind". The prefix *ke-* here marks something accidental — a pattern you have already seen in *kepeksa* and *kebablasen* in unit 8.

**Tak terké** = *tak* + *terké* (take someone somewhere), "I'll take you". The form *tak*, which has appeared a few times already, is fully explained in unit 18; for now, just recognize that *tak* + verb means "I'll (do it)".
**Pancèn** means "indeed, really"; the krama is also *pancèn*. It is used to agree firmly: *pancèn ngono* (that's just how it is), *pancèn apik* (it really is good).

grammars.title: Seven question words
body: They all stand **in the place of the thing being asked about**; they don't have to go at the start of the sentence, unlike English, which moves them to the front.
after: **Kapan is the same at both levels** — one word you don't have to learn twice.
**Pripun** is the short form of *kadospundi* and by far the more common in real conversation. If you learn only one, learn *pripun*.
A question word can be followed by *waé* to mean "all, any": *nyang ngendi waé?* (where all did you go?), *sapa waé?* (who all?), *apa waé?* (what all?).

grammars.title: Yes-no questions: three ways, all correct
body: For questions answered "yes" or "no", Javanese has three ways, used interchangeably.

head: Method
Example
Note
rows: a little more emphatic or formal
very common at food stalls and markets

after: **One word is enough as an answer**: *iya* / *ora*, *wis* / *durung*, *ana* / *ora ana*, *gelem* / *ora*. Answering with a full sentence sounds as if you are being interviewed.
Note that the pair is **wis … durung** (already … not yet), not **wis … ora**. Offering the wrong pair makes your question sound odd.

sections.title: When you didn't catch the answer

blocks.text: This is the part of the unit you will use most in real life, and textbooks almost never teach it. Javanese speakers talk fast and often use madya (a middle speech level) that you won't know. These sentences buy you time without stopping the conversation.

blocks.title: Mudheng: the most useful word in this unit
items: *Mudheng* means "to understand, to get it", and it is different from *ngerti*, "to know". *Aku ngerti* = I know (the information). *Aku mudheng* = I understand (the explanation).
Saying *aku durung mudheng* is far better than nodding while confused, and Javanese speakers welcome it — they will repeat more slowly, or switch to Indonesian.
The krama is *mangertos*, and you will often hear it as a question: *sampun mangertos?* (do you understand?).

blocks.text: This pattern almost never fails in Java, and it always has the same four parts:

items: **Nuwun sèwu** — excuse me. Opens the door.
**Badhé nyuwun pirsa** — I'd like to ask. Says what is coming.
**The question** — as short as possible, in as much krama as you can manage.
**Matur nuwun** — thank you, whatever the answer.

blocks.text: A complete example: *Nuwun sèwu, Pak. Badhé nyuwun pirsa. Stasiunipun wonten pundi, nggih? … Matur nuwun sanget.* Four sentences, and you have asked like someone who grew up there.

How much is the cheapest one?

answers: Sapa — ngendi — pira — Kapan — Ngapa — Piyé
Menika punapa? — Ingkang rawuh sinten? — Panjenengan tindak pundi? — Reginipun pinten? — Pripun caranipun?
Nuwun sèwu, malih? — Kula dèrèng mangertos. — Alon-alon, nggih. — Menika tegesipun punapa? — Kula namung saged sekedhik.
Kamar iki luwih amba tinimbang sing kuwi. — Sing paling murah pira? — Larang banget. — Rada ciyut, ning adhem. — Aku seneng sing anyar.
